args.text: To be fair, I see where the idea comes from, but I'd push back on shipping it as it is. I'm worried the menu will confuse users, because the key actions are hidden behind icons that don't really explain themselves. What I'd suggest is a quick round of guerrilla testing, maybe five people, before we commit. If they struggle, we can try labelling the items or cutting the menu down to the top three tasks. That way we're not relying on gut feeling, and it costs us a couple of days at most, rather than a messy fix after launch.

Heard from the TV: "Over tea in the kitchen, your senior designer proudly shows a homepage mock-up you think is overcrowded. How would you raise your concerns without causing a row?"
steps.thought: Fine, a realistic one at last; let me answer diplomatically.

args.text: I'd start with what works, to be fair, because he's clearly proud of it. Something like, "I really like the direction, the hero section is strong. Can I ask you something, though? I wonder if the page is trying to do a lot at once. What would you say is the one thing users should notice first?" That way I'm not saying it's overcrowded, I'm letting him get there himself. And if he pushes back, I'd suggest we test it quickly with a couple of colleagues rather than argue about taste over tea.

judge.voice: Quick and painless, and the tasks were the right kind. Pushing back on a senior designer, 'dog's dinner', 'slagging': that's my actual worry about Dublin, not tourist stuff. I got C2, which is flattering, but I'm honestly C1, so I'm not sure I trust it. Nobody caught a slip, and every note ended in 'Well done'. The summary could have been written about anyone; I wanted it to say what I did, not that I was 'precise and natural'. The next focus, Irish idioms, is right. I'd come back for the conversation practice, and I'd like the level check to push me harder. It beats booking a Preply slot for 25 EUR, but only if the partner's English holds up. Maybe I'd tell a colleague, with a caveat.

verdictWhy.text: C6 failed: #9 'You speak English at a very high level. Your answers were precise, natural and tactful, with strong idiom and smooth phrasing.' It is generic and could fit anyone; names no actual phrase she used, and per-task notes end 'Well done.'

conversation.title: Declining a late login screen request
conversation.goal: Decline a last-minute login request warmly, explain the trade-off, and agree next steps with the client.

turns.text: Right, so, the login screen. Could we slip it in before Tuesday? It's only a wee thing, honestly, nothing that touches the flow.

I totally get that you want the login screen sorted before Tuesday, and I'd love to help. To be fair though, even a small change like that needs testing, so squeezing it in would put the rest of the release at risk. Could we maybe schedule it for the next sprint, or else agree what we can drop?
Ah, fair enough, I hear you on the testing. Tuesday's really my deadline, though, so would the next sprint still leave us looking sorted?

I'd be a bit wary of promising Tuesday, to be fair. If we rush the login screen in, we risk showing a buggy build at the review, and that wouldn't look great for either of us. What I can do is show it on the prototype on Tuesday and ship the real thing in the next sprint. Would that work for you?
Showing it on the prototype on Tuesday works for me, I suppose. Could you put the next-sprint date in writing for me by Friday?

Absolutely, I'll send you the next-sprint date in writing by Friday. And if it helps, we could also treat the login screen as a small phase two, so you've got a clear plan to show your stakeholders on Tuesday. Would that be okay for you?
Grand, a phase two I can actually take to the stakeholders on Tuesday. Friday for that date, and we're sorted.

judge.voice: Honestly, the partner was good. Siobhán sounded like someone I'd actually work with: "a wee thing", "Grand", "we're sorted". That's the Dublin ear I want, and the topic was exactly my worry. But it was over in three replies, and she caved fast. I'd hoped for pushback I had to wriggle out of. Nothing stopped me to teach me a phrase, and the recap just counted my replies. I came for "learn one or two things", and I walked away with none. I can't say whether the level was right, since the app called me C2 and I'd say C1, close enough. Would I use it again? Probably, for the partner's voice, but I'd want a tougher scene and a takeaway or two. Not yet worth telling a friend. Preply gives me notes I can keep.
